title: Spider Mites & Hemp Russet Mite: Magnification, Webbing & Look-Alikes

content.overview: Spider mites and hemp russet mites can both injure leaves but differ greatly in body form, visibility and webbing. Specialist work depends on magnification and direct mite evidence because russet-mite injury can overlap disease, nutrition and environmental disorders.

vocabulary.definition: A mite in groups such as Tetranychus that commonly lives in colonies on leaf undersides and may produce visible silk webbing.
Aculops cannabicola, a very small eriophyid mite associated with Cannabis that requires high magnification for reliable detection.
A group of extremely small plant-feeding mites with an elongated body and two pairs of legs in the adult form.

sections.title: Webbing is useful but absence does not end the mite differential
sections.body: Webspinning spider mites commonly produce silk on infested tissue and can be viewed with a hand lens. Hemp russet mites are much smaller, do not produce the characteristic spider-mite webbing and generally require stronger magnification. Use these differences to direct the next observation rather than assuming all mite injury looks the same.

sections.title: Russet-mite confirmation needs magnification
sections.body: Hemp russet mites are microscopic and their injury can resemble other biotic or abiotic problems. Extension guidance recommends direct observation under suitable magnification for confirmation. Record the plant part sampled and method used because a negative low-magnification inspection is weak evidence against a microscopic mite.

sections.title: Preserve the evidence gaps
sections.body: Peer-reviewed work on hemp russet mite continues to note knowledge gaps in biology, damage quantification and management efficacy. Specialist education should not convert those gaps into universal thresholds or guaranteed controls. Separate what is directly observed from what is inferred and what still requires validation.

workedExamples: Stippling with obvious webbing and mobile mites on leaf undersides supports a spider-mite diagnosis more directly than the same stippling without organism evidence.
Upward leaf distortion with no webbing can keep hemp russet mite in the differential, but microscopy is needed before presenting the mite as confirmed.
commonMistakes: Using absence of visible mites to rule out hemp russet mite when magnification was inadequate.
Treating all stippling or leaf curl as a mite diagnosis.
Publishing a universal hemp-russet action threshold when the source literature does not establish one.
content.practicalApplication: Compare two suspect samples under the appropriate magnification. Record webbing, body form, number of visible leg pairs when resolvable, plant location, distribution and injury. State what evidence would be needed to confirm or reject each mite hypothesis.
content.summary: Spider mites and hemp russet mites require different detection expectations. Webbing, magnification and direct organism evidence help discriminate them, while unresolved knowledge gaps must remain visible in the decision record.
